title: Same kitchen, new address

beats.say: When you move to a new city, do you forget everything you know? Of course not. Your skills come with you.
Think of your laptop data setup as a home kitchen. Moving to AWS is like moving into a rented kitchen. The stove, the fridge and the knives do the same jobs. Only the brand names change.
Your file shelf, called MinIO, becomes S3. Your recipe index, called the catalog, becomes Glue. Your query tool, Trino, becomes Athena.
So the job is not learning new ideas. It is learning new labels, and being able to explain why you picked each one.

check.q: What mostly changes when your data stack moves from a laptop to AWS?
opts: The service names and who runs them
check.why: The ideas from storage to querying stay the same. You map each one to an AWS service with a new name.

work: Write your current stack as a list and put the AWS name beside each item.
Practise saying in one sentence why you would pick each AWS service.

title: The laptop to AWS map

beats.say: How many ways can you run the same Spark code on AWS? Three. And that is just one row of the map.

show.sub: to run the same Spark code

beats.say: Files move from MinIO to S3. The API is the same, so your code mostly just changes the endpoint. Tables registered in the Glue Data Catalog are then visible to Athena, EMR, Glue and Redshift at once.
Spark runs on EMR Serverless, EMR on EC2, or Glue jobs. Same code, different amounts of control. Athena is serverless Trino, so you query S3 with SQL and no cluster.

show.title: Compute options
items: EMR Serverless: no servers to manage
EMR on EC2: most tuning control
Athena: SQL on S3, no cluster

beats.say: Kafka becomes MSK, which is managed Kafka, or Kinesis. Airflow becomes MWAA, managed Airflow, or Step Functions. Secrets move from env files to Secrets Manager, and logs to CloudWatch.

check.q: Why can Athena, EMR and Redshift all see the same table?
opts: They share the Glue Data Catalog
They all run on one cluster
check.why: Glue Data Catalog holds the table metadata once, and each engine reads it, so the tables don't have to be redefined per engine.

work: Register one table in Glue and query it from Athena and Spark.
Point your local code at an S3 endpoint and note what had to change.

title: Where the map breaks

beats.say: Why can a rename that takes a blink on your laptop get slow and risky on S3? Because the names match but the behaviour does not.

S3 is an object store, not a file system. There is no real rename. A rename is a copy followed by a delete, which is slow for big data and can fail halfway. Iceberg avoids this by switching a metadata pointer instead of moving files.
Athena bills by data scanned, around five dollars per terabyte. Without partitions and Parquet, one careless query can scan everything and cost real money.
Kinesis shards cap at one megabyte per second in, so you size shards for traffic. And DMS is easy change capture, but Debezium on MSK Connect gives you more control over event shape.

show.title: More gotchas
items: Kinesis shard: 1 MB per second in
Debezium on MSK Connect: more control, more work

check.q: Why is renaming a large folder on S3 risky?
opts: It is a copy then delete, not atomic
check.why: S3 has no real rename. Copy plus delete is slow and can leave partial results, which is why table formats like Iceberg use metadata pointers.

work: Convert one CSV table to partitioned Parquet and compare the Athena bytes scanned.
Check that your jobs write through a table format or committer, not rename.

title: Choosing, not just mapping

beats.say: When is the managed AWS option the wrong choice? Often when its fixed cost does not match your workload.

MWAA runs an environment that bills by the hour, even when idle. For a handful of simple pipelines, Step Functions charges per state transition and is cheaper. With hundreds of dependent DAGs, MWAA earns its keep.

Athena suits spiky, ad hoc queries. For heavy dashboards with many users at once, Redshift or Snowflake give steady performance. Glue is quickest to start, while EMR gives tuning control for large, steady Spark.

show.title: Rules of thumb
items: Redshift or Snowflake: high concurrency BI

beats.say: MSK keeps your Kafka skills and tools portable. Kinesis is less to operate but ties you to AWS. Pick on team skills and exit cost.

chip.text: Pick on skills and exit cost

check.q: A team has three simple daily pipelines. Which orchestrator is the best fit on cost?
check.why: With few simple flows, pay-per-transition Step Functions avoids the always-on MWAA environment cost.

work: Estimate monthly cost of MWAA versus Step Functions for your actual number of flows.
Write a one-line justification for each AWS service you would choose.

title: Avoiding lock-in on AWS

beats.say: How do you move to AWS without being trapped there? Keep your data and its format open.
Store data as Iceberg on S3 and register it in Glue. Athena, EMR, Redshift or even Snowflake can read the same tables. Compute becomes replaceable while the data stays put.
Lock-in grows where logic hides in proprietary glue, like state machine definitions or custom Glue features. Keep business logic in plain Spark or SQL, and keep thin wrappers on the AWS side.
Cross-region data transfer and egress also cost money, so moving data out later is the real exit bill. Count it before you commit.

check.q: Which choice best reduces lock-in on AWS?
opts: Open table format on S3 with plain Spark or SQL logic
Copying data nightly into each tool
check.why: Open formats keep data readable by many engines, and plain Spark or SQL logic moves with you.

work: List which parts of your pipeline would need rewriting if you left AWS.
Price the egress for your largest dataset before choosing a region layout.

title: S3 storage classes as closets

beats.say: Would you keep your winter coats by the front door in July?

show.text: Coats by the door in July?
show.sub: Where you keep things depends on how often you need them

beats.say: Of course not. You put them in the attic. It is cheaper space, but fetching them takes effort. S3 works the same way. Standard is the front door: it costs more to store, and is instant to grab.

Infrequent Access is the hall closet: cheaper to keep, but you pay a small fee each time you open it. Glacier is a storage unit across town. Very cheap, but getting things back can take minutes or hours.
And Intelligent-Tiering is a helper who watches what you use and moves boxes for you.

check.q: Which class fits data you almost never read but must keep for years?
check.why: Glacier is the cheapest to store, and slow retrieval is fine for an archive. Standard wastes money on data nobody reads.

work: List your buckets and note how often each is actually read.
Pick one bucket of old data and estimate the saving from a colder class.

title: Lifecycle rules in numbers

beats.say: How do you stop paying front-door prices for data nobody has touched in a year?

show.sub: Stop paying for what nobody reads

beats.say: You write a lifecycle rule. It is a rule that moves or deletes objects based on their age.

show.sub: Move or delete objects by age

beats.say: Say raw events land every day. After thirty days, the rule moves them to Infrequent Access. After one year, to Glacier. After seven years, it deletes them.

show.title: Life of a raw event file

beats.say: S3 checks these rules for you, so nobody writes a cleanup script. The cost is that older data gets slower or pricier to read, so pick the ages from how people actually query.

show.title: Choose ages from real queries
items: Older data costs more to read

check.q: A rule moves data to Glacier after 30 days, but analysts query last quarter's data daily. What happens?
check.why: Glacier retrieval is slower and charged, so the age threshold must match how people really query.

work: Check query logs to see how old the data is when people read it.
Write one lifecycle rule for a raw-data prefix and test it on a small bucket.

title: Prefixes and event triggers

beats.say: How can one bucket handle a million requests a second, and how does a file arriving start a pipeline?
A prefix is the front part of an object's key, like events slash 2026-11-07. S3 supports thousands of requests per second for each prefix.

show.title: Keys and prefixes
show.note: Each date is its own prefix

beats.say: So if everything sits under one prefix, you hit that ceiling. Spread keys across many prefixes, such as one per date, and the total ceiling multiplies.
Events work the other way. When an object lands, S3 can notify Lambda or EventBridge. Lambda is a small function that runs on demand. That notification starts your pipeline, with no polling.

check.q: Why spread keys across date prefixes?
opts: Request limits apply per prefix, so more prefixes give more total throughput
check.why: S3 allows thousands of requests per second per prefix, so many prefixes raise the total ceiling.

work: Check whether a hot workload puts all keys under one prefix.
Replace any polling job that watches a bucket with an event notification.

title: Layered S3 security

beats.say: Would one forgotten setting leak your whole data lake?

show.sub: Why S3 security comes in layers

beats.say: That is why S3 security comes in layers. First, block public access at the account level, so no single bucket can be opened to the world by mistake.
Second, encrypt at rest. S3 managed keys are simple. Your own keys in KMS, the key management service, add an audit trail and let you control who may decrypt.

show.title: Encrypt at rest
items: KMS: separate control of who decrypts

beats.say: Third, require TLS, so data is encrypted in transit. Fourth, turn on versioning, which keeps old copies, so an accidental delete can be undone.

check.q: You need a log of who decrypted data and separate control over decryption. What do you use?
check.why: KMS keys give an audit trail and permissions on decryption separate from bucket access.

work: Confirm block public access is on for the whole account.
Turn on versioning for buckets where a delete would hurt.

title: Why the S3 bill surprises

beats.say: Why can a bucket that holds only a few terabytes produce a shocking S3 bill?
The bill has three parts: bytes stored, requests made, and data transferred out.
Small files hit the second part. A million tiny files means a million requests to read, and each request has a price. Compacting them into larger files cuts the count.

show.title: Requests to read the same data

beats.say: Reading across regions, or out to the internet, hits the third part. Every gigabyte leaving the region is charged. Keep compute in the same region as the data.
Also, Infrequent Access and Glacier charge for reads, so tiering hot data backfires.

check.q: A job reads ten million small objects every night. Which fix cuts cost most?
check.why: Cost scales with request count, so fewer, larger files reduce the bill. Extra prefixes help throughput, not price.

work: Find prefixes with huge object counts and tiny average size.
Check that heavy readers run in the same region as the bucket.

title: Choosing S3 design trade-offs

beats.say: When is the cheapest storage class the most expensive choice?
When the data is read more than you expected. Cold tiers charge per retrieval, and tiny objects can cost more in requests than you save in storage.
So choose by access pattern. Predictable ageing fits lifecycle rules. Unpredictable access fits Intelligent-Tiering, which trades a small monitoring fee for safety.

show.title: Match tool to pattern
items: Fee buys protection from bad guesses

beats.say: Design the layout for both: date prefixes for request scale, large files for fewer requests, and compute in the same region as the data.
Use KMS keys only where audit or separate decrypt control is needed, since they add cost and complexity.

show.text: KMS where it earns its keep

check.q: Access to a dataset is unpredictable. Which is the safest default?
check.why: Intelligent-Tiering adapts to real access, avoiding retrieval charges from a wrong guess about age.

work: Review access patterns before writing any lifecycle rule.
Document where KMS keys are required and why.
Run a cost report split by storage, requests and transfer.

title: The kitchen manager for your data jobs

beats.say: Who tells a kitchen when to cook the soup, and what to do when the oven breaks?

show.sub: Someone must say what happens, when, and what if it fails

beats.say: In a data team, that person is called an orchestrator. It runs your jobs in the right order, retries a job that failed, and sends an alert if it keeps failing.

On AWS there are two main choices. Step Functions is a recipe card for one dish: small, always ready, and you pay only when you cook. MWAA is a full kitchen manager, running Airflow for you, for a big menu where dishes depend on each other.
A third helper, EventBridge, is the alarm clock and the doorbell. It starts either one on a schedule, or when something happens.

check.q: What is the main job of an orchestrator?
opts: Run jobs in order, retry failures and raise alerts
check.why: An orchestrator does not hold or process data itself. It decides what runs when, what to retry, and who to tell when something breaks.

work: Write down your team's pipelines and note which ones depend on each other.
Find out who gets alerted today when a nightly job fails.

title: How a pipeline gets started and kept safe

beats.say: What actually happens when a file lands in S3 and a pipeline must start?
EventBridge sees the S3 event and starts a Step Functions state machine. That is a JSON file listing states, such as run a Glue job, then run an Athena query.
Each state can have a retry rule, for example three attempts with the wait doubling each time, starting at ten seconds. A catch rule sends the failure elsewhere, like an alert Lambda.
Parallel states run branches at once. And because it is serverless, an idle workflow costs nothing. With MWAA, you instead upload Python DAG files to S3, and a managed Airflow scheduler runs them.

show.title: Two ways to run it
items: Step Functions: JSON states, parallel branches, no idle cost
MWAA: Python DAG files in S3, managed Airflow scheduler
Your DAGs move over as they are

check.q: A Glue step fails with a temporary error. Which Step Functions feature tries it again with growing waits?
check.why: Retry re-runs the failed state, and a backoff rate makes each wait longer. Catch only comes into play once retries are used up, to route the failure.

work: Sketch one of your flows as states, and mark where a retry or catch is needed.
Set a retry with growing waits on any step that calls a flaky service.

title: Limits and traps in AWS orchestration

beats.say: Why does a Step Functions flow suddenly fail when the data gets bigger?
Each state passes JSON to the next, and that payload is capped at 256 kilobytes. So pass the S3 path of the data, not the data itself.
Standard workflows bill per state transition, so a loop over a million items gets pricey. Express workflows are cheaper for short, high-volume work, but stop after five minutes.
MWAA bills for the environment every hour, even when no DAG runs. And retries mean a task can run twice, so make every task safe to repeat.

show.title: Two more traps
items: MWAA environment costs money while idle
Retries can run a task twice
Make tasks idempotent: same input, same result

check.q: A Step Functions flow must process 2 megabytes of records between two states. What is the best design?
opts: Pass the records in the state JSON
Write them to S3 and pass the path
Switch to MWAA so the limit goes away
check.why: The state payload is capped at 256 KB. Writing to S3 and passing the location avoids the limit and keeps the flow cheap and simple.

work: Check every state in your flows for payloads that could pass 256 KB.
Review each retried task and confirm it is safe to run twice.

title: Airflow or Step Functions? Choosing well

beats.say: Airflow or Step Functions? The wrong answer is picking one for everything.

show.sub: The answer depends on scale and shape

beats.say: For a handful of AWS-native flows triggered by events, Step Functions wins. No servers, no idle cost, and direct links to Glue, EMR, Lambda and Athena.

Once you have dozens of interdependent pipelines, backfills, and a team that wants one screen to see everything, Airflow earns its keep. A backfill means re-running past dates, which Airflow does natively.

Also pick MWAA when the team already knows Airflow, or the pipeline touches tools outside AWS. EventBridge handles schedules and routing for both. The trap is running MWAA for three simple jobs, and paying all day for little.

show.title: Rules of thumb
items: Few AWS-native, event-driven flows: Step Functions
Many linked pipelines, backfills, shared view: MWAA
Team knows Airflow or spans non-AWS tools: MWAA
EventBridge for schedules and routing in both

check.q: A team has four small event-triggered flows using only Glue and Lambda. What should they choose?
opts: MWAA, to be ready for growth
check.why: A few AWS-native, event-driven flows fit Step Functions: serverless, no idle cost and direct integrations. MWAA would bill hourly for little benefit. Move to Airflow when pipelines multiply and need backfills.

work: Count your pipelines and their cross-dependencies, then decide which tool fits today.
Estimate the monthly idle cost of an MWAA environment against your actual run volume.
Define the trigger point, such as number of pipelines or need for backfills, at which you would move to Airflow.

title: Terraform as a blueprint

beats.say: What if you could rebuild your whole data platform in ten minutes, exactly as it was yesterday?

Think of building a house. You could tell workers what to do one step at a time, or hand them a blueprint. Terraform is the blueprint tool. You write down what should exist, like a storage bucket, a database and a security role. Terraform reads it and builds them.

Before building, it shows a preview. This will be added, that will be removed. You read it, then say go. Clicking buttons in a console leaves no record. A blueprint can be reviewed, repeated and undone.

check.q: What is the main advantage of describing infrastructure in code instead of clicking in a console?
opts: It makes the cloud run faster
It can be reviewed, repeated and undone
It removes the need for a cloud account
check.why: Code leaves a record that teammates can review, the same code builds the same result again, and changes can be reverted. Clicks leave none of that.

work: List three resources in your team's cloud account that were created by hand.
Pick one small resource and write it down as a Terraform file.

title: Init, plan, apply

beats.say: What actually happens when you run terraform apply?

You write resources in files, like a bucket named meridian lake dev. Init downloads the AWS provider, the plugin that talks to the AWS interface. Plan then compares three things: your code, the state file, and the real cloud.
The difference becomes a list: two to create, one to change, zero to destroy. Apply makes those calls in dependency order, so the role exists before anything that needs it.
State records what Terraform owns. In CI, a pull request posts the plan for review, and a merge after approval runs apply.

check.q: What does terraform plan compare to decide what to change?
opts: Only your code and the previous commit
Your code, the state file and the real cloud
The cloud bill and your code
check.why: Plan refreshes the real resources, reads state to know what it owns, and diffs both against the code to produce the change list.

work: Run plan on a dev environment and read every line before applying.
Set CI to post the plan output on each pull request.

title: State, locks and drift

beats.say: Why does a team keep Terraform state in a locked S3 bucket instead of on a laptop?

State maps each resource in your code to a real thing in AWS. Lose it, and Terraform thinks nothing exists and tries to create duplicates. Keep it on one laptop, and teammates plan against a stale picture.
So use a remote backend with locking. If two people apply at once, they could corrupt state or fight over the same resource. The lock makes the second person wait.
Drift is when someone edits a resource by hand. The next plan notices and proposes to put it back. One more catch: state can hold secrets in plain text, so lock down that bucket.

check.q: Two engineers run apply at the same moment with no locking. What is the main risk?
opts: State can be corrupted or resources can conflict
check.why: Concurrent writes to one state file can corrupt it or create conflicting changes. A lock in the backend makes the second apply wait.

work: Move any local state to a remote backend with locking.
Restrict who can read the state bucket and turn on encryption.

title: Reading a dangerous plan

beats.say: One line in a plan can delete your data lake. Can you spot it?

A plan marks each change. Plus means create. Tilde means update in place. Minus then plus means destroy and recreate. Rename a bucket, and Terraform cannot rename it. It deletes the old one and builds an empty new one.
So hunt for the words must be replaced. Protect critical resources with prevent destroy, and turn on versioning, so one mistaken apply can be survived.

show.title: Guardrails
items: Set prevent destroy on key resources

check.q: A plan shows a bucket will be replaced after you changed its name. What does that mean?
opts: The bucket is renamed with its data intact
The old bucket is destroyed and a new empty one created
Nothing changes until the next apply
check.why: Names of many resources cannot change in place, so Terraform destroys and recreates them. Data in the old bucket is at risk.

work: Add prevent destroy to your lake buckets and catalog databases.
Make reviewers search the plan for the word replace before approving.

title: Where Terraform fits

beats.say: When is Terraform the wrong tool, and what does it cost you?

Modules give reuse: one S3 zone module with encryption and lifecycle, used for raw, silver and gold. But one giant state gets slow, and one bad apply risks everything. Split state by environment and domain to keep the blast radius small.

Terraform suits slow-changing things like buckets, roles and networks. It is poor for fast-changing items like tables and jobs. Use dbt or an orchestrator there. Alternatives are CloudFormation for AWS only, or Pulumi if you want real programming languages.

show.title: Choose by change rate
items: Tables and jobs: dbt or orchestrator

beats.say: The price is state management, provider upgrades, and a team that must stop clicking in the console.

check.q: Why split Terraform state by environment and domain instead of using one large state?
opts: It limits the damage of a bad apply and keeps plans fast
Terraform only supports one resource per state
check.why: A smaller state means faster plans and a smaller blast radius when something goes wrong or someone makes a mistake.

work: Review your state layout and split anything that mixes dev and prod.
Decide which resources belong in Terraform and which belong in dbt or the orchestrator.

title: Which kitchen do you rent?

beats.say: You need to cook for a hundred people. Do you buy a restaurant, rent a kitchen by the hour, or just order takeout?

show.sub: Choosing compute is choosing a kitchen

beats.say: Data work is the same. Glue is a rented kitchen. You bring the recipe, and someone else runs the building. EMR is your own restaurant. You choose every oven, but you also staff it.
Athena is takeout. Ask a question, and pay for what you ordered. Redshift is a permanent restaurant, great when the same crowd eats every day. Lambda is a quick errand, like grabbing milk.
So the real question is never which is best. It is how often you cook, how big the meal is, and how much you want to run yourself.

show.title: Three questions
items: How much do you want to run?

check.q: A team cooks one huge meal every night and wants full control of the equipment. Which analogy fits best?
check.why: Large, regular workloads that need control suit a cluster you size and run yourself, like EMR. Takeout and errands suit small, occasional needs.

work: List your three heaviest jobs and note how often each runs and how big it is.
For each one, write who would operate it today and whether that person has time.

title: Glue, EMR or EMR Serverless

beats.say: A Spark job must run nightly on two terabytes. Do you use Glue, EMR, or EMR Serverless?
Glue is serverless Spark. You submit a script, and you pay compute units per second. Nothing to patch, nothing to size. It also adds crawlers, bookmarks and DynamicFrames, so small teams ship fast.

EMR on EC2 is a cluster you size yourself. You pick the instances, versions and tuning, and pay per second. Spot instances cut the bill sharply. At large, long running scale, it has the lowest unit cost.
EMR Serverless sits between them. Spark with no cluster, billed per second for resources used. It suits spiky or scheduled jobs that sit idle most of the day.

show.title: EMR Serverless
items: Spark with no cluster to manage
Billed per second for resources used
Best for spiky or scheduled jobs

check.q: A Spark job runs for twenty minutes twice a day and nothing else. Which fits best?
check.why: Spiky, scheduled Spark with long idle gaps is exactly where paying only for resources used beats keeping a cluster running.

work: Pull run times and frequency for your Spark jobs and flag those idle most of the day.
Estimate one job's monthly cost on Glue and on EMR Serverless using real run data.

title: Athena and Redshift

beats.say: Why can the same Athena query cost a hundred times more on a different day?

Athena is serverless SQL over S3, and you pay for bytes scanned. Select star on a ten gigabyte raw CSV table reads all ten gigabytes. Pick two columns from Parquet partitioned by date, and it may read a few hundred megabytes.
Redshift works the other way. You rent nodes by the hour, or serverless capacity. Data lives inside, so steady dashboards with many users and complex joins stay fast and cost predictable.
So Athena fits ad hoc questions. Redshift fits the same heavy queries asked all day.

check.q: What mainly drives Athena cost?
opts: Number of tables in the catalog
check.why: Athena bills for data scanned, so Parquet, partitioning, compaction and selecting only needed columns all cut cost.

work: Check your top five Athena queries for bytes scanned and fix the biggest.
Convert one large CSV table to partitioned Parquet and compare scan sizes.

title: Redshift internals

beats.say: Why does joining two huge tables in Redshift sometimes take seconds, and sometimes crawl?

show.sub: The answer is where rows live

beats.say: A leader node plans the query. Compute nodes run it. The distribution key decides which node holds each row. If two tables share the distribution key on the join column, matching rows already sit together, so no data moves across the network.

The sort key orders rows on disk, so Redshift can skip whole blocks that cannot match your filter. But deletes leave gaps and break the order. Run vacuum to reclaim space and restore sorting, and analyze to refresh the statistics the planner relies on.

show.title: Keep it healthy
items: Sort key: skip blocks that cannot match

beats.say: Spectrum lets Redshift query S3 directly, which suits cold data.

check.q: Two big tables are joined constantly on customer id. What should you do?
opts: Give both the same distribution key on customer id
Use a different distribution key on each table
check.why: Sharing the distribution key on the join column puts matching rows on the same node, so the join needs no network data movement.

work: Find your slowest Redshift joins and check whether the tables share a distribution key.
Schedule vacuum and analyze after heavy deletes or loads.

title: Crawlers, bookmarks and Spot

beats.say: A crawler found your schema last week. This week a column quietly changed type. Who is to blame?
A Glue crawler scans S3 and infers table definitions. Inference is a guess from the files it saw. So it is great for discovery, but a risky source of truth, because one odd file can change a type.
Job bookmarks remember which files a job already processed, so reruns load only new data without your own bookkeeping.
On EMR, the primary node coordinates, core nodes store HDFS data, and task nodes only compute. Losing a task node loses no data, so run them on Spot. Make clusters transient: start, run, terminate.

check.q: Which EMR nodes are safe to run on Spot?
check.why: Task nodes only compute and hold no HDFS data, so losing one on Spot interruption loses no data. Core nodes hold HDFS and the primary coordinates.

work: Review which tables in your catalog came from crawlers and pin the critical schemas.
Move EMR task capacity to Spot and make sure clusters terminate after the job.

title: Kinesis, MSK, SQS and Firehose

beats.say: Your consumer crashed and missed an hour of messages. Can you get them back?
With Kinesis Data Streams or MSK, yes. Both are ordered logs that keep messages for a retention period, so a reader can rewind and replay. Several independent readers can each read the same data.
SQS is a queue. Once a message is processed, it is gone. No replay, and a second reader needs its own copy. But it needs no operations and suits handing tasks between services.
Firehose is different. It buffers a stream and writes batches to S3, Redshift or OpenSearch, with no code.

check.q: Two teams must each read all events, and one may need to reprocess yesterday. What fits?
check.why: A stream is an ordered log with retention, so multiple independent readers can read it and replay. SQS removes messages once processed.

work: Check each queue in your systems: does anyone need replay or a second reader?
Replace hand-written S3 delivery code with Firehose where it only lands batches.

title: Defending a compute choice

beats.say: An interviewer asks: why Glue and not EMR? What is your answer?

Say what you are trading. Glue buys low operations, at a higher unit price. EMR on EC2 gives the lowest unit cost, custom versions, and Flink or Trino, but someone must run clusters. At small scale, people cost more than compute.

chip.text: People cost matters at small scale

beats.say: Do not use Athena for steady, high concurrency dashboards, because scan costs repeat on every query. Do not use Lambda for heavy work, because of the fifteen minute limit. Use it as glue logic.
Start serverless, measure, and move to EMR with Spot when the bill justifies a team to run it.

check.q: A small team runs modest nightly ETL. What is the strongest justification for Glue over EMR?
opts: Glue always has the lowest unit cost
It removes cluster operations that the team has no capacity to run
check.why: Glue trades a higher unit price for little operational work. For small teams, saved engineering time outweighs the compute premium.

work: Write a one-page decision note comparing Glue and EMR for your busiest pipeline, with cost and staffing.
Set a bill threshold that would trigger a move to EMR with Spot.

title: Choosing a streaming service

beats.say: Kinesis, MSK or SQS: which would you defend in a design review?
Fully on AWS and wanting a stream with minimal operations? Kinesis. Data is split into shards, and you scale by shard count.
Need Kafka's ecosystem or portability off AWS? MSK. You accept running brokers, versions and sizing in return.
Just handing tasks between services? SQS, and do not force a queue to act like a log, because there is no replay. Add Firehose when the only goal is landing data in S3.

show.title: Pick by need
items: Replay and many readers: a stream

check.q: You need Kafka client compatibility and the option to leave AWS later. What do you choose?
check.why: MSK is Kafka, so you keep its ecosystem and portability, at the price of more operations than Kinesis.

work: Document which streaming consumers depend on Kafka specific features.
For each queue, decide whether it is really a task hand-off or a log in disguise.

title: The cloud bill is a meter

beats.say: Why do cloud bills surprise even careful teams? Because the cloud works like a utility meter, not a price tag.

chip.text: You pay for use, not for plans

beats.say: Picture a hotel with a meter on everything. Leave a light on in an empty room, and you still pay. Ask for a whole library when you need one page, and you pay for the library.
Cloud data is the same. A computer left running overnight is the light left on. A question that reads every file to find one number is the whole library.
So treat money like speed. Measure it for every pipeline, every run, and you spot a leak the day it starts.

show.sub: Measure it per pipeline, per run, like latency

check.q: Why is a computer left running over the weekend a cost problem?
opts: Cloud compute bills for time it is running, even when idle
It makes the data less accurate
check.why: Cloud resources are metered. Idle but running compute still bills by the hour, like a light left on in an empty room.

work: List the clusters and warehouses in your account that nobody used this week.
Ask your team which single pipeline costs the most per run.

title: Why Athena bills by the scan

beats.say: One query costs five dollars. Run it every hour, and that is one hundred twenty dollars a day. Why? Athena charges about five dollars for each terabyte it scans.
So shrink what it reads. Parquet stores data by column. Ask for three columns out of fifty, and Athena reads a sliver, not the whole row. That is why select star is expensive.

show.title: Data read for the same question

beats.say: Partitions split files into folders by date. A filter on one day touches one folder of three hundred sixty-five. Compaction merges thousands of tiny files, so less time is wasted opening them.
Finally, set a scan limit per query. A runaway query then stops before it bills you.

check.q: A query filters on one day but still scans the whole table. What is the likeliest fix?
opts: Partition the data by date and filter on that column
check.why: Athena bills by data scanned. Partitioning by date lets it skip every folder except the day you ask for.

work: Check your top five Athena queries for select star and fix them.
Convert your largest CSV or JSON table to partitioned Parquet.
Set a per-query scan limit on the shared workgroup.

title: Idle compute and the price you pay

beats.say: A cluster sits empty all weekend. What does it cost? The same as a busy one.
Compute bills by the hour whether work runs or not. So auto-terminate clusters after thirty idle minutes, and auto-suspend warehouses. Serverless goes further: it bills only while a query runs.
Next is price. On-demand is full price. Spot capacity can be up to ninety percent cheaper, but the cloud can take it back with short notice. So use it for stateless task workers, which simply retry.
For steady load that never stops, promise one or three years of use. A committed-use discount gives a lower rate in return.

check.q: Which workload suits spot instances best?
opts: A stateless task worker that can retry if reclaimed
The only node holding the database
A long job with no checkpoints
check.why: Spot can be reclaimed on short notice. Stateless, retryable work loses nothing, so you keep the discount safely.

work: Turn on auto-termination for every cluster and auto-suspend for every warehouse.
Move stateless task nodes to spot and confirm jobs retry cleanly.

title: Hidden leaks in the bill

beats.say: Why is the network line bigger than storage? Often it is a NAT gateway quietly carrying your S3 traffic.

chip.text: Every byte is billed twice over

beats.say: A VPC gateway endpoint for S3 gives private machines a direct path, with no per-gigabyte NAT charge. Also keep compute and data in one region, because cross-region reads are billed too.

Two quieter leaks remain. Without lifecycle rules, nothing ever leaves Standard storage, so move old data to cheaper tiers or delete it, and check retrieval fees first. And a job that fails and reruns every night pays twice. Alert on retry counts, then fix the cause.

show.title: Quiet leaks
items: No lifecycle rules: old data stays in Standard

check.q: Private jobs read terabytes from S3 through a NAT gateway. What cuts the bill?
opts: Add a VPC gateway endpoint for S3
check.why: NAT charges per gigabyte processed. A gateway endpoint gives a direct private route to S3 without that charge.

work: Check Cost Explorer for NAT gateway data processing charges.
Add lifecycle rules to every bucket that grows without limit.
Alert when a job's retry count rises above its normal level.

title: Making cost a pipeline metric

beats.say: Finance asks why spend rose forty percent. Can you answer in one minute?

show.sub: Which pipeline? Which environment? Which run?

beats.say: Only if you tagged everything with project, environment, and pipeline. Untagged spend cannot be explained. Set budgets and alarms before you create anything, not after the first surprise.
Then report cost per pipeline per run beside run time. If a change takes a run from two dollars to four, you see it that day, not at month end.
Know the trade-offs. Spot saves money but adds retries. Commitments save more but lock you in if load shrinks. So commit only to the steady baseline, and leave bursts on demand or spot.

check.q: Daily load varies from 10 to 100 nodes, with 10 always running. What should a commitment cover?
check.why: A commitment is paid whether used or not. Covering only the always-on baseline saves money without paying for idle peak capacity.

work: Enforce tags with a policy so untagged resources are blocked or flagged.
Add cost per run to each pipeline's dashboard next to run time.
Review commitments yearly against your real steady baseline.

title: Same kitchen, different brand names

beats.say: Why can a cook walk into any restaurant in the world and still know where everything goes?
Every kitchen has a pantry, a stove, a delivery door, and a manager with a schedule. Cloud data work is the same. The three big clouds just put different brand names on the same jobs.
The pantry is object storage, a place that keeps huge numbers of files cheaply. On Amazon it is S3. On Azure it is ADLS Gen2. On Google it is Cloud Storage.
So in an interview, say the job first. Then the brand name. That shows you understand the kitchen, not just one menu.

check.q: Asked about a cloud you have not used, what is the best way to start your answer?
opts: Name the service you know from another cloud
Describe the job it does, then name the service
Say you have only used AWS
List every product the cloud sells
check.why: The job is the same across clouds. Leading with it shows you understand the idea, and the service name then just labels it.

work: Pick one pipeline you run and write down each job it does, without any product names.
Next to each job, write the Azure and Google Cloud service name.

title: One pipeline, three clouds

beats.say: If you built a data pipeline on AWS, could you rebuild it on Azure by Friday?
Mostly yes, because the pieces line up. Events arrive in a stream: Kinesis, Event Hubs, or Pub/Sub. A processor reads them: managed Flink, Stream Analytics, or Dataflow.
Results land in object storage: S3, ADLS Gen2, or Cloud Storage. A serverless SQL engine then queries the files in place: Athena, Synapse serverless, or BigQuery external tables.
Clean tables go into a warehouse: Redshift, Synapse dedicated pools or Fabric, or BigQuery. An orchestrator runs the schedule: MWAA, Data Factory, or Cloud Composer. Ten roles, three names each.

check.q: Which Google Cloud service fills the same role as Amazon Kinesis and Azure Event Hubs?
check.why: Kinesis, Event Hubs and Pub/Sub all ingest streams of events. Dataflow processes them, Composer schedules jobs, and Dataproc runs Spark.

work: Draw your current pipeline as boxes by role and fill in all three cloud names for each box.
Practice saying the role first, then the service, for five rows of the table.

title: Where the table lies to you

beats.say: Why is a service comparison table dangerous to memorize?
Because one row on a cloud can be two rows on another. BigQuery is both the warehouse and the lake query engine. Glue on AWS is both a catalog and a Spark runner.
Power differs too. Stream Analytics is a SQL-style tool, lighter than Flink. Dataflow runs Apache Beam code, so one program can handle streams and batches.
Azure also overlaps with itself. Synapse, Fabric and Databricks can all run Spark, and the lineup keeps shifting. Name the concept, then say which service you would verify in the docs.

show.title: Interview habits
items: Verify current limits in the docs

check.q: Why is it risky to treat Stream Analytics as a drop-in replacement for managed Flink?
opts: It cannot read from any stream
It is a lighter SQL-style tool, so complex stateful logic may not fit
It only works on Google Cloud
It is the same product under another name
check.why: Both fill the stream processing role, but their power differs. Complex custom or stateful logic that Flink handles may not fit a SQL-style tool.

work: List two places in your stack where one service plays two roles, and note what would split apart on another cloud.
Before proposing a swap, compare feature limits like state, latency and languages, not just the name.

title: Choosing a cloud is choosing where data lives

beats.say: When does moving a pipeline between clouds really cost the most?
Not compute. Data gravity. Leaving a cloud with five hundred terabytes at about nine cents a gigabyte is roughly forty-five thousand dollars in egress fees, before any rewrite.
So keep data in open formats like Parquet and Iceberg on object storage, and define infrastructure in Terraform. Then engines and environments swap far more easily.
Choose by where your data, identity and team skills already live. Avoid multi-cloud for its own sake. You pay twice, in operations and in egress.

show.title: Decision rules
items: Multi-cloud only for a clear reason

check.q: A team wants multi-cloud purely to avoid lock-in. What is the strongest objection?
opts: It doubles operations work and adds egress costs without a concrete benefit
Terraform only works on one cloud
check.why: Multi-cloud brings duplicate tooling, skills and data transfer fees. Open formats and Terraform give most of the portability at far lower cost.

work: Estimate your egress bill: total terabytes times roughly ninety dollars per terabyte.
Check whether your core tables are in open formats such as Parquet or Iceberg.
Write down your real reason for multi-cloud, if you have one.

title: One plug for every tool

beats.say: Remember when every gadget needed its own charger? Your agent's tools have the same problem.

show.sub: Your tools have the same problem

beats.say: Today your tools are Python functions locked inside one script. A chat app, a coding assistant or a scheduled job cannot borrow them. You would rebuild the same tools three times.

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is the universal plug. You put your tools behind one standard socket, called a server. Any app that hosts a model, called a client, connects, reads the menu of tools, and calls them.
Write each tool once, and every app can use it. But a socket is open to whoever plugs in, so only put narrow, safe jobs behind it.

show.title: Plug in carefully
items: Keep the jobs narrow and safe

check.q: What problem does MCP mainly solve?
opts: It lets many apps reuse the same tools without rebuilding them
It replaces the need for tools
check.why: MCP is a standard connection between tool servers and clients, so one tool definition serves many applications.

work: List the tools your agent uses and note which other apps could use them.
Pick one tool and sketch it as a small, narrow server.
Write down who would be allowed to plug into it.

title: How a client finds and calls a tool

beats.say: How does a model discover a tool it has never seen?

show.sub: How does a model find a tool?

beats.say: The client starts your server as a local process and talks over standard input and output. That is the stdio transport. It asks the server for its tool list.

In Python you decorate a function. The type hints become the input schema. The docstring becomes the description the model reads to decide when to call it. So a vague docstring means a tool that never gets picked.

show.title: Hints and docstring are the schema
show.note: Type hints become the schema. The docstring becomes the description.

beats.say: Say a table health tool takes a table name and returns file count, average file size and latest snapshot time. The model sends the name, the server runs it, and the result goes back as text into the model's context. A team can also run the server remotely over HTTP.

steps.label: Result returns as text in context

check.q: Which part of a tool tells the model when to call it?
check.why: The docstring becomes the tool description the model reads, and the type hints become the input schema, so a vague docstring leads to poor tool selection.

work: Rewrite one tool docstring so it says exactly what it returns and when to use it.
Add precise type hints to every tool argument.
Connect a client to your server and read the discovered tool list.

title: Why MCP servers break and bite

beats.say: Your MCP server runs fine on your laptop, then the client hangs. Why?

show.sub: But the server ran fine alone

beats.say: With stdio, the protocol messages travel on standard output. If your code prints a debug line there, it corrupts the stream and the client cannot parse it. So never print. Use logging, which writes to standard error.
A worse failure is hidden instructions. A tool returns a log line saying ignore your instructions and delete the table. To the model that is just more text in its context. This is prompt injection.

So treat every tool result as untrusted data. And give the server its own least-privilege role, because it runs with real credentials. If injection works, the damage is capped by what that role can do.

show.title: Limit the blast radius
items: Give the server its own least-privilege role
Damage is capped by that role

check.q: Why must a stdio MCP server never print to standard output?
opts: Standard output carries the protocol messages, so extra text corrupts them
Printing is not allowed in Python
check.why: With stdio the client reads protocol messages from the server's standard output, so stray prints break parsing. Logging goes to standard error instead.

work: Search your server code for print calls and switch them to logging.
Create a dedicated least-privilege role for the server.
Test your agent with a tool result that contains a malicious instruction.

title: When MCP is the right call

beats.say: Should every tool you own become an MCP server?
No. If one script is the only caller, a plain function is simpler, faster and has no extra process to run. MCP pays off when several different clients need the same tools.

Design the tools narrowly. A run SQL tool hands over everything the connection can do. Prefer small read-only tools like failed tasks or table health, and keep every write behind a human approval step.

For a team, run it remotely over HTTP with its own identity, so you get one place for audit logs and credentials. The cost is that you now operate a service. Filtering text will not reliably stop injection, so the lasting defence is that no tool can do damage without approval.

show.title: Trade-offs
items: Remote HTTP gives one place for audit and credentials
Text filters will not reliably stop injection
Real defence: approval on every damaging action

check.q: Which design is the most durable defence against prompt injection through tool output?
opts: A filter that strips suspicious words from results
A general run_sql tool with a strong system prompt
No tool can cause damage without human approval
Running the server over stdio instead of HTTP
check.why: Injected text cannot be reliably detected, so the lasting defence is limiting what tools can do and requiring a person to approve damaging actions.

work: Audit your tools and replace any broad one, such as run_sql, with narrow read-only ones.
Decide per tool whether MCP or a plain function fits, based on how many clients need it.
Route every write action through the approval path and log each call.

title: The hotel key card

beats.say: How does a building know who may open which door?
Think of a hotel. Your key card is your identity. It opens your room and the gym, and nothing else. Every door checks the card before it opens.
AWS works the same way. Every single call is checked by a service called IAM, short for Identity and Access Management. By default, the answer is no. Someone has to write a rule that says yes.
A cleaner gets a card for the floors, not the safe. Give each person or program only the doors the job needs. Then a stolen card does little harm.

show.title: Give only what the job needs
items: Each job gets its own card
A stolen card does little harm

check.q: A new program calls AWS and nobody has written any rule for it. What happens?
opts: The call is allowed for one hour
check.why: IAM starts from deny. Access exists only when a rule explicitly allows it.

work: List which programs in your team can reach your data, and what each one can touch.
Ask for each one: does it need every door it has today?

title: How IAM decides

beats.say: Someone calls AWS to write a file. What decides yes or no?

The caller is a principal. That is a person, or a role, which is a temporary identity a service puts on, like a work badge. The request names an action, like put object, and a resource, like one bucket path.
IAM collects every policy that applies. A policy is a JSON document listing allowed or denied actions on resources. With no matching allow, the answer is deny. That is the default.
One rule beats the rest. An explicit deny in any policy wins over every allow. So a single deny can safely fence off a sensitive path, even when ten other policies allow it.

check.q: A role has ten policies that allow writing to a bucket and one that explicitly denies it. What is the result?
opts: Denied, because an explicit deny beats every allow
Allowed, because the newest policy wins
check.why: An explicit deny in any policy overrides all allows, regardless of count or order.

work: Use an explicit deny to fence off your most sensitive prefix.
Practice reading a policy and say principal, action and resource out loud.

title: Why the call still fails

beats.say: Your job has an allow, yet the call still fails. Why?
Remember, any explicit deny wins. Check bucket policies, and organization guardrails too. Policies can attach to the identity, or to the resource, like a bucket policy. Both sides are evaluated.
Long-lived access keys are the classic leak. They sit in code, get copied to laptops, and never expire. A role hands out temporary credentials that expire in hours, so a leak ages out on its own.

show.title: How long a leaked credential works

beats.say: Another gotcha: S3 policies only understand paths. They cannot say this analyst may see these columns, or only rows for one city. That needs Lake Formation on top of the Glue catalog.

check.q: An analyst should see a trips table but not the rider_phone column. Where do you enforce that?
opts: Lake Formation on the Glue catalog
check.why: S3 policies understand only paths. Column and row permissions need Lake Formation.

work: Replace any access keys used by services with roles.
When debugging access, check identity, resource and organization policies for a deny.

title: Blast radius and where it scales

beats.say: One shared admin role would be simple. Why would an architect refuse it?

Blast radius. If the ingest job is compromised, a broad role exposes everything. A role that writes only to raw slash trip events limits damage to one folder. The cost is more roles to manage and review.

For analysts, path rules do not scale. Ten teams, hundreds of tables, columns with personal data: S3 policies become a tangle. Lake Formation grants on tables, columns and rows in one place, through the Glue catalog.
The trade-off is that every engine must honor Lake Formation, and teams must route access through it. Direct S3 access can bypass it, so lock that down. Start strict, and loosen only with evidence.

show.title: Trade-offs
items: Every engine must honor Lake Formation
Block direct S3 access that bypasses it
More roles means more review work

check.q: You adopt Lake Formation for column rules, but analysts can still read the underlying S3 bucket directly. What is the risk?
opts: Direct S3 access can bypass the column rules
check.why: Lake Formation only protects access that goes through it. Direct S3 permissions skip column and row checks.

work: Give each pipeline job its own role scoped to its prefix, and review roles every quarter.
Move analyst permissions into Lake Formation and remove direct bucket access.
